docs.title: Operations Building Block
docs.text:
These pages describe operations for the eoepca-demo cluster: how to check a problem, restore a service, and prepare for platform changes. They cover the deployed tools and the checks still needed before sign-off.

The work is divided into three areas:

Discipline Main question EOEPCA page Security Operations Is the platform protected, and are security events detected and handled? Security Operations Reliability and Remediation Operations Are user services healthy, and can service be restored safely? Reliability and Remediation Operations Platform Lifecycle and Continuity Operations Can the platform be changed, supported, recovered, and retired safely? Platform Lifecycle and Continuity Operations

A security finding may need a software update, which must then be deployed and checked for service failures. In cases like this, the team responsible for the immediate risk leads the work, with help from the other teams.

docs.title: Operator Reference
docs.text:
The Operating Model explains how an incident moves from Inspect to Investigate and Act, with Verify as part of Act and Learn after recovery. The Monitoring Stack, Dashboards and Usage, and Alerting and SLOs describe the tools used during that work.

For worked examples, follow a slow request in STAC Service Path, or a session or data problem in Workspace Monitoring. When Kubernetes API Traffic Rises follows extra controller activity through the API charts, Keep alert, and Grafana markers.

docs.title: Alerting and SLOs
docs.text: The demo sends Prometheus alerts through Alertmanager to Keep. Platform rules cover conditions such as disk pressure and missing targets; SLO alerts cover service quality, such as slow requests.

docs.title: Prometheus, Alertmanager, and Keep
docs.text: Prometheus evaluates rules against collected metrics. When an alert fires, Alertmanager groups it with related alerts and sends a notification to Keep. Routing, silences, and inhibition in Alertmanager determine which notifications reach Keep.

docs.title: Why Use Keep?
docs.text:
A slow Kubernetes API can delay both workspace creation and processing jobs. Reviewing their alerts together in Keep helps an operator see a possible shared failure. Assignment and acknowledgement show who has taken the work, so another operator can see its status or take it over.

For API/etcd and STAC alerts, Keep saves measurements when the notification arrives. The Grafana link opens the surrounding period for comparison with metrics and logs. The control-plane example shows this for API load and etcd latency, including the saved snapshot and chart markers.

docs.title: Baseline Alerts
docs.text:
The baseline rules live in _rules/baseline-alerts.yaml. They cover platform-level concerns such as:

  • missing Prometheus targets
  • Prometheus ingest problems
  • rule evaluation failures
  • node pressure and disk exhaustion
  • crash looping pods
  • replica mismatches
  • persistent volume exhaustion

Service-specific rules add checks for request quality and application behaviour to these platform alerts.

docs.title: Recording Rules and Alert Rules
docs.text:
A recording rule saves a calculated metric for reuse. For example, the control-plane rules record API request rate and an earlier hourly baseline. Grafana can show both on the same chart.

An alert rule checks whether a condition needs attention. The API traffic alert requires traffic to exceed both a minimum rate and twice the earlier baseline for a sustained period. Separate rules check API errors, availability, and etcd latency. A traffic spike alone does not show service impact or its cause.

Chart thresholds need to follow rule changes so that an operator can still see why the alert fired.

docs.title: Alert Context
docs.text: Enrichment adds measurements and investigation links to an alert. Keep saves them with the alert, so the operator can use the same starting information even after the condition has passed.

docs.title: Keep for Alert Enrichment
docs.text:
The Keep connection and workflows are defined in:

  • alertmanagerconfig-keep.yaml
  • keep-alertmanager-relay.yaml
  • app-keep.yaml

Alerts arrive with the labels and annotations from their rules. Three native YAML workflows use these settings to add investigation links, save an optional metrics snapshot, and write firing/resolved events. The API/etcd and STAC SLO rules specify which dashboard and measurements to use.

Prometheus records a small set of context measurements every 30 seconds as operations:alert_context. Keep reads the selected dashboard’s measurements once for a new firing occurrence. It saves the result in metrics_context and the receipt time in metrics_context_at. Repeated notifications, acknowledgement, and resolution retain the snapshot. If the query fails after one retry, the context stays unavailable.

The control-plane example explains the API/etcd signals. The STAC example follows the gateway, auth proxy, API, and database.

The keep AlertmanagerConfig sends firing and resolved notifications to:

http://keep-alertmanager-relay.operations.svc.cluster.local/alerts/event/prometheus

Earlier routes send selected noisy workload alerts to a null receiver. The remaining alerts use the default Keep receiver.

docs.title: Keep Events in Grafana
docs.text:
The API/etcd and STAC dashboards place firing and resolved notifications next to the measurements as chart markers. They reach Grafana through the log collection path:

  1. When a covered Prometheus alert fires or resolves, the native Keep workflow writes a structured event to the backend Pod log.
  2. Alloy collects that log and sends it to Loki with the cluster, namespace, and container labels.
  3. Grafana’s Keep events annotation query selects those entries from Loki for the dashboard’s time range. Each returned entry becomes a chart marker.

Each log entry contains event_type: keep_alert_event, the dashboard ID, alert name, status, and Keep link. Grafana selects the entries for its own ${__dashboard.uid}. It reads chart measurements from Prometheus and markers from Loki. The saved snapshot stays with the alert in Keep.

Only firing and resolved events produce markers; assignment and acknowledgement remain in Keep. Native change filters skip ordinary repeated notifications, but do not guarantee exactly one marker per event. The markers therefore give an investigation timeline rather than a complete audit of response actions.

See Keep Events for the toggle, marker contents, and checks for missing events. The annotation query is maintained in kubernetes-api-and-etcd.json.

docs.title: Shared Configuration
docs.text:
Each alert selects a context profile with dashboard: stac or dashboard: control-plane. Its dashboard_url points to the Grafana dashboard. Keep uses the profile to query measurements and reads the dashboard ID from the URL for chart markers. Changing an ID in the dashboard JSON can break existing bookmarks and alert links.

Add context_snapshot: "true" to save measurements when a new occurrence fires. To cover another service, define its context recording rules and set the profile and dashboard URL on its alerts. The Keep workflows stay the same.

Public URLs are set in the dashboard links, alert rules, and Keep configuration. The deployment reference explains the settings and checks. The workflows use built-in Keep providers. MySQL retains alert state across backend Pod replacements; the demo has no database backup or restore guarantee.

docs.title: SLOs
docs.text: An SLO sets a service target, such as a maximum share of slow requests. It measures the result that users receive. CPU and memory metrics can help explain a failure or delay, but do not measure that result directly.

docs.title: Burn Rate
docs.text:
Burn rate shows how fast a service uses its error budget. A high value means that it will miss its target sooner if the problem continues.

For example:

stac_get_latency_500ms_burn_rate_1h > 14.4

The STAC latency target is 99% of requests within 500 ms. This leaves a 1% error budget for slow requests.

The burn-rate rule divides the observed slow-request ratio by the allowed 1% budget. A burn rate of 1 means the service is using the budget at the allowed rate. A burn rate of 14.4 means it is using the budget 14.4 times faster.

For a 30-day SLO window, sustaining a 14.4 burn rate would use the whole 30-day error budget in about two days:

30 days / 14.4 = 2.08 days

The one-hour record detects a rapid increase in slow requests. The six-hour record helps detect a problem that persists for longer.

The deployed STAC rules are defined in stac-alerts.yaml. The live stac-alerts PrometheusRule contains:

  • one-hour and six-hour request-latency burn-rate records for STAC GET and POST requests
  • matching upstream application and APISIX gateway burn-rate records for diagnosis
  • a PostgreSQL mean execution latency record for database correlation
  • warning alerts where the six-hour request burn rate is above 6 for 30m, unless the one-hour critical condition is already true
  • critical alerts where the one-hour request burn rate is above 14.4

Alerts fire on the request-level GET and POST records. The upstream, gateway, and database records help locate the layer that contributes to the delay.

The STAC dashboard shows the public-route records above separate proxy and backend metrics. Their values can differ because they measure different points in the request path.

docs.title: From Alerting to Remediation
docs.text:
The investigation determines which response is suitable. The planned remediation-action library will define approved procedures with limits and recovery checks; it is still in development.

A change is complete only after the service request works again and the relevant measurements confirm recovery. If the problem remains, the operator returns to investigation. The action and result belong in the incident record, along with any alert or dashboard changes needed for the next incident.

docs.title: Observability Basics
docs.text: When a request is slow, a latency chart shows when the problem started. Logs can then show which component reported a delay or error. An alert brings a condition to an operator’s attention; an SLO sets the service quality expected by users. Together, these support Inspect and Investigate in the operating model.

docs.title: Observability In Practice
docs.text:
Each source answers a different question:

Signal Main question Role in the operating model Metrics Is the service healthy, fast, or overloaded? Inspect trends and service quality; find affected components Logs What exactly happened? Investigate requests, errors, and component behaviour Alerts Does someone need to act now? Notify the operator of a condition that needs attention SLOs Is the service still delivering acceptable quality? Focus Inspect on user impact and urgency

docs.title: Metrics
docs.text:
Metrics record values over time, such as request duration or memory use. They help answer questions such as:

  • is request latency rising?
  • is the error rate increasing?
  • are pods hitting CPU or memory limits?
  • how quickly is an error budget being consumed?

These values show whether a problem is growing and which components are busy. They usually cannot explain why a particular request failed.

docs.title: Logs
docs.text:
Logs record individual events. After finding a rise in errors on a chart, an operator can look at logs from that period to find:

  • which request failed
  • which component generated the error
  • what payload, tenant, or collection was involved
  • what changed just before the incident

An error message can help explain the symptom, but it may also be a result of a failure elsewhere. The timing, affected requests, and other measurements help establish whether it explains the problem.

docs.title: Alerts
docs.text:
An alert calls for attention when a measured condition needs a response. Its rule should:

  • indicate a problem that matters
  • identify the affected service and give a useful starting point
  • avoid firing on every transient spike

Repeated notifications that need no action make important alerts harder to see. Rules need review when this happens, or when a service fails without an alert.

docs.title: SLOs
docs.text:
A Service Level Objective (SLO) defines acceptable service quality in measurable terms. For STAC, the latency target is 99% of GET and POST requests within 500 ms. The remaining 1% is the error budget for slow requests.

An SLO can also set a target for availability or request errors. It helps the operator judge the effect on users and how soon a response is needed.

docs.title: Why EO Platforms Need This
docs.text: A slow data request can involve the gateway, application, database, or infrastructure. Different teams may own these components. A shared timeline of measurements, logs, and changes helps them investigate the same problem. The operating model gives them a common process for choosing a change and checking that users can use the service again.

docs.title: When Kubernetes API Traffic Rises
docs.text:
Kyverno, Crossplane and other controllers read and update Kubernetes objects as they work. More controller activity can raise API traffic. The control-plane charts show which resources and clients are busy, and whether errors or etcd latency rise with the traffic.

For this example, we temporarily increased reconciliation in Crossplane’s Kubernetes provider. API traffic rose from about 88 to more than 220 requests per second. KubeAPIRequestSpike fired after traffic stayed above the threshold for five minutes, and Alertmanager sent it to Keep. API 5xx errors stayed at zero. The alert rules stayed unchanged.

docs.title: Review the Alert in Keep
docs.text:
In the Keep alert feed, look for KubeAPIRequestSpike or an etcd latency alert. When you take an alert, assign it to yourself and acknowledge it so other operators can see that someone is handling it.

Keep enriches a new firing alert with a snapshot of API traffic, its earlier baseline, etcd latency, busy resources, and Crossplane and Kyverno activity. The alert’s Grafana link opens charts for that period, while the saved values remain in Keep after acknowledgement and resolution.

Open the alert, select View Alert, then enable Enriched Fields Only to see the saved links and measurements.

The screenshot shows the saved measurements for KubeAPIRequestSpike.

docs.title: Compare Events with the Charts
docs.text:
Follow the alert’s Grafana link to compare the saved values with the charts before and after the notification. If you open the Kubernetes API and etcd dashboard directly, set its time range to the incident period.

Keep events is on by default. It adds blue markers when Keep handles a firing or resolved notification. Hover over a marker to see its time, status, and link back to the alert. These markers come from Keep’s event log, which Alloy sends to Loki for Grafana to read. The saved measurements stay in Keep.

Turning Keep events off gives the same charts without the markers, as shown below. This only changes the display; metrics and alert delivery continue.

Signal What to check API traffic and earlier baseline Did traffic rise before errors or latency? Request errors Are API or backend requests failing? Etcd latency Is the API waiting for its database? This is backend request latency measured by the API server. Busy API resources Which resource types and operations account for the requests? Crossplane and Kyverno requests Which measured clients were busy? Control-plane disk writes Did node storage latency rise in the same period?

The resource breakdown shows which API objects were accessed. Client metrics and logs are needed to identify the callers. A rise in traffic may help explain a stall, but storage latency can also matter. Compare the timing with care: markers show when Keep logged the notification, including delivery delay.

docs.title: Check Recovery
docs.text:
Returning the provider to its normal settings reduced API traffic. The alert resolved when the five-minute request average fell below the threshold.

If workspaces or processing jobs were also affected, retry them before closing the incident. Their completion checks that users can work again. API errors and latency should also return to normal, and controllers should resume their work.

The Keep record should explain what changed, whether it helped, and which measurements were missing. If the problem is limited to STAC requests, the STAC scenario follows that request path in more detail.

The dashboard guide covers missing markers. The alerting reference explains the shared workflows and snapshot limits. The deployment sources contain the rules and dashboard.

docs.title: Dashboards and Usage
docs.text: Grafana dashboards show service behaviour and the components behind it. The dashboard for the reported problem is usually the best starting point, with the time range set to include the first symptom and any recent change.

docs.title: How Dashboards Are Provisioned
docs.text:
The dashboards are generated as ConfigMaps under argocd/eoepca/operations/parts/_dashboards and labeled with grafana_dashboard: "1".

Grafana loads them automatically, so no manual import is needed. Each dashboard has the baseline tag. Public links are set in the manifests, and stable dashboard IDs preserve bookmarks and alert links. The configuration reference explains how Keep uses those links.

The live operations namespace contains dashboard ConfigMaps for:

  • curated-prometheus-overview
  • curated-k8s-resources-cluster
  • curated-k8s-resources-node
  • curated-k8s-resources-pod
  • curated-control-plane
  • curated-crossplane
  • curated-security-compliance
  • curated-stac-slo
  • workspaces-overview

The Compliance dashboard combines Kyverno policy results and Trivy scan findings. It replaces the separate policy-audit and Trivy dashboards.

docs.title: Prometheus
docs.text:
Source: prometheus.json

When monitoring data is missing or looks wrong, this dashboard helps check Prometheus itself. It shows target discovery and sync, scrape failures, appended samples, query rate, and storage state.

docs.title: Kubernetes Cluster
docs.text:
Source: kubernetes-cluster.json

This dashboard compares namespaces by CPU and memory use, requested and limited capacity, and network and storage activity. It helps locate an affected namespace when the report does not yet identify a workload.

docs.title: Kubernetes Pods
docs.text:
Source: kubernetes-pods.json

Once the namespace is known, the Pod dashboard shows container CPU use and throttling, memory working set against requests and limits, and network and disk activity. These measurements help narrow the investigation to a workload or container.

docs.title: Kubernetes Nodes
docs.text:
Source: kubernetes-nodes.json

Node capacity and scheduling pressure can explain why workloads do not start or run slowly. This dashboard is also useful when several affected workloads share a node.

docs.title: Kubernetes API and etcd
docs.text:
Source: kubernetes-api-and-etcd.json

The demo dashboard shows API traffic against its earlier baseline, API errors, availability, and etcd latency. Resource views show what the API handles. Crossplane and Kyverno client activity helps identify measured sources of requests.

When several services report errors or resource creation becomes slow, these charts can show a shared API or etcd problem. Controller activity needs to be compared over the same time range before attributing load to a controller. The control-plane scenario explains the investigation and the links between Keep alerts and Grafana chart markers.

docs.title: Crossplane Reconciliation
docs.text:
Source: crossplane-reconciliation.json

The demo dashboard shows reconciliation rates and p99 duration for Datalab and Storage composition controllers and provider managed-resource controllers. Error panels show the total for the selected period and errors per minute. The Provider selector filters provider charts. CRD gate controllers are excluded.

Rates and p99 duration use five-minute windows. Composition counts include periodic checks and runs triggered by watched changes. They combine all resources of each type; they do not identify an individual workspace or the trigger for a run. Successful scheduled requeues are not errors.

docs.title: STAC
docs.text:
Source: stac.json

The STAC dashboard follows the request path from APISIX ingress to stac-auth-proxy and eoapi-stac. The ingress section shows public request and server-error rates, request/upstream/gateway p99, and GET/POST latency budget burn. Separate proxy and backend sections use each service’s own counters and histograms to show:

  • the share of GET and POST requests within 500 ms over 30 days
  • latency error budget use and one-hour and six-hour burn rates
  • request rate, HTTP 5xx errors, and p99 latency
  • mean query latency for the shared eoapi database in the backend section

The target is 99% of requests within 500 ms. A burn rate above one uses the budget faster than allowed; more than 100% budget used exceeds the target. Periods without traffic show no data. Proxy and backend counts include some of the same requests, so adding them would count requests more than once. The alert rules measure the public APISIX route.

docs.title: Compliance
docs.text:
Source: compliance.json

This dashboard brings Kyverno policy results together with Trivy vulnerability, exposed-secret, configuration, RBAC, and compliance findings. Critical findings appear first, followed by action tables for secrets and access, image updates, and deployment configuration. Before a change, the matching Trivy or Kyverno report is needed to confirm the affected image or resource and the report age.

The main views show:

  • critical findings that need review first
  • high and critical image vulnerabilities and secret findings
  • configuration and access findings
  • failed policy rules and evaluation errors
  • collection errors, report ages, exceptions, and cluster controls

Repeated workload reports for the same image count once per image and namespace. Secret findings come from image scans, not scans of live Kubernetes Secrets. Cluster controls and ClusterRole findings apply to all namespaces.

The collapsed review section contains scan health and exception details. Zero findings are meaningful only when the expected workloads have fresh reports; a missing scan can also leave the total at zero.

docs.title: Workspaces
docs.text:
Source: workspaces.json

The workspace selector compares running sessions, CPU and memory use, requested PVC storage, and owned buckets for one or more workspaces. Each workspace includes its main, session, and control-plane namespaces. The dashboard opens with 24 hours of history.

Managed data panels show HTTP requests, successful and failed presigned URL requests, transfer bytes, and collection health. Activity totals cover the selected period. Requested PVC storage is allocated capacity; transfer bytes measure data movement. Neither measures stored data.

The workspace scenario explains the session counts, recording rules, PodMonitor, and a short investigation example.

docs.title: Keep Events
docs.text:
Both Kubernetes API and etcd and STAC have a Keep events control, enabled by default. With the incident period selected, it places alert notifications on the charts alongside the measurements.

On time-series charts such as API traffic and etcd latency, blue lines and small markers show these events. Hover over a marker for the alert name, firing or resolved status, time, and Open alert in Keep link. Both states use blue, so the status text distinguishes them. Stat cards and tables have no markers. If the link opens only Keep’s feed, the matching alert can be selected there.

For example, EtcdRequestLatencyHigh: firing marks a notification handled by Keep. A later EtcdRequestLatencyHigh: resolved marks its recovery notification. The measurements around these points show what was happening when Keep handled each notification. Each marker is a separate event; the chart does not shade the whole incident period.

Turning off Keep events hides the markers. Alerts still reach Keep, and the metric charts continue to work. Assignment, acknowledgement, and response notes stay in Keep. The saved metrics snapshot also stays with the alert.

Grafana reads up to 100 matching log entries for the selected period. If there are more events, a shorter range is needed to see them. Marker times come from the workflow log and include alert delivery and processing delay.

If markers are missing, check the same period in Grafana Explore with the Loki data source:

{namespace="operations",container="keep"}
  | json | event_type="keep_alert_event"

No matching events can mean that no covered alert changed state, or that the workflow or log collection failed. Check the workflow execution in Keep and the Alloy/Loki collection path. Marker history follows Loki log retention. If Keep history is cleared, older markers can remain after their linked alerts have been removed. The dashboard_uid field identifies the target dashboard; each dashboard’s query selects it with ${__dashboard.uid}. The Kubernetes API and etcd dashboard also reads the earlier event format to retain history. The alerting reference describes the workflows that produce these events. Grafana calls the marker query a Loki annotation query.

docs.title: Typical Operator Usage
docs.text:
An alert’s dashboard link provides a starting point. For a user report without an alert, the affected service determines where to start: STAC for searches, Workspaces for sessions and managed data, or Compliance for scan and policy findings. Missing or inconsistent measurements need a Prometheus check first.

For a broader resource problem, Kubernetes Cluster helps locate the namespace, then Kubernetes Pods gives container detail. Kubernetes Nodes helps when the affected workloads share a node or show scheduling pressure. If workspace creation and several controllers fail together, API/etcd charts may reveal a shared dependency problem. Crossplane Reconciliation helps check controller rates, duration, and errors when managed resources are slow to become ready.

Loki logs and source scan or policy reports provide details behind the charts. The STAC and control-plane scenarios show this investigation with Keep and Grafana screenshots.

docs.title: Dashboard Checks
docs.text:
• Set the time range to include the first symptom and the most recent relevant change.
  • Match the service, namespace, workload, and route filters across the panels being compared. These dashboards cover the single eoepca-demo cluster.
  • Treat an empty panel as unknown until you confirm the target, query, and data source.
  • Open the source metric, log, policy report, or scan report before you approve a change.
  • Reuse the same dashboard and filters during Verify so that before-and-after evidence is comparable.

docs.title: Monitoring Stack
docs.text: The monitoring tools run in the operations namespace of eoepca-demo. Prometheus metrics and Loki logs are available together in Grafana, while Keep holds alerts and their response records. Deployment sources are in eoepca-plus/argocd/eoepca/operations.

docs.title: Deployed Components
docs.text:
The main components are:

Component What it does When it helps Prometheus Collects metrics and evaluates rules. Its queries show trends; target status helps explain missing measurements. Grafana Shows metrics and logs in dashboards. Charts place service and component behaviour on the same timeline. Alertmanager Groups alerts and routes notifications. Routing, silences, inhibition, and delivery status can explain a missing notification. Loki Stores searchable logs. Request and component events can explain a symptom found in metrics. Grafana Alloy Forwards Pod and selected node-service logs; API audit collection is configured but unverified. Collection checks help when an expected source is absent from Loki. Keep Stores alerts, saved measurements, and response status. An operator can see related alerts, who is handling them, and what was saved when they arrived. Keep OAuth2 Proxy Restricts access to the Keep interface. It checks the user’s Keycloak roles before allowing access. Keep relay Adapts Alertmanager webhooks to the Keep event endpoint. Relay errors can explain why a delivered webhook has no matching Keep alert.

The deployment definitions are under parts/monitoring and parts/alerting.

docs.title: Prometheus
docs.text:
Prometheus scrapes platform and application targets, then evaluates the baseline, service, and workspace rules against those measurements. The stored time series supply dashboards, recording rules, and alerts.

The retention and persistence settings are defined in app-kube-prometheus-stack.yaml.

docs.title: Grafana
docs.text: Grafana uses OIDC login and has Prometheus and Loki data sources. This lets an operator compare a metric trend with request errors or component events from the same period without moving to a separate log tool.

docs.title: Alertmanager
docs.text: Alertmanager groups repeated alerts and routes their notifications to Keep. If an expected alert is missing there, its routes, silences, inhibition rules, and delivery status are the first part of the notification path to check.

docs.title: Loki
docs.text:
Loki stores workload and selected node-service logs. An API audit collection path is also configured in Alloy, but delivery of those records remains unverified. The current deployment uses:

  • a single-binary Loki setup
  • object storage on S3-compatible backend
  • a chart-managed ServiceMonitor for Loki metrics
  • Loki canaries to exercise the log pipeline

See app-loki-stack.yaml.

docs.title: Grafana Alloy
docs.text:
Alloy runs as a DaemonSet on each node. It sends Kubernetes Pod logs and selected node-service journal records to Loki, with labels such as namespace, pod, container, and app. Its API audit pipeline is configured to normalize and forward audit events, subject to the delivery gap noted above.

The pipeline is defined in monitoring/alloy/config.alloy.

docs.title: Keep
docs.text:
Keep brings related alerts and their response status into one place. For API/etcd and STAC alerts, it also saves measurements and Grafana links, so the assigned operator does not have to rebuild the initial queries. This is useful when several services fail together, as in the control-plane scenario.

For API/etcd and STAC alerts, a shared Keep workflow writes firing and resolved events to the backend log. Alloy sends these to Loki. Grafana reads them as chart markers, with links back to Keep. The alerting reference describes the event path.

docs.title: Use the Stack During an Incident
docs.text:
An alert’s time and affected service give the investigation a starting point. Its Grafana link opens the relevant charts, if one is configured. For a user report without an alert, the service dashboard is the starting point. The charts show whether the symptom is visible at the gateway, application, workload, or a shared dependency; Loki can then supply event and request details for that period.

When expected data is missing, the collection path needs checking before the data can support a decision. Prometheus target status, Alloy, and Loki canaries help distinguish a quiet service from a collection failure.

After a change, repeating the user’s operation tests recovery. Comparing the same metric and log queries before and after the change helps confirm the result. Pod readiness alone cannot show that the service works for users.

docs.title: Public Operator Endpoints
docs.text:
The public endpoints use Keycloak login:

  • Grafana at https://monitoring.develop-v2.eoepca.org, requiring a monitoring:grafana_admin, monitoring:grafana_editor, or monitoring:grafana_viewer role in Keycloak
  • Keep at https://alerting.develop-v2.eoepca.org/alerts/feed, requiring an alerting:keep_admin or alerting:keep_noc role in Keycloak

These endpoints are exposed through APISIX routes:

  • monitoring/routes.yaml
  • alerting/routes.yaml

The ServiceMonitors and PodMonitors page explains scrape configuration. The STAC and workspace examples show how to use the measurements during an investigation.

docs.title: Operating Model
docs.text: A reported failure can pass through several components before it reaches the user. This model describes how an operator follows that problem, chooses a change, and checks whether it helped. Monitoring provides measurements and logs; service knowledge helps the operator interpret them.

docs.title: Operating Rules
docs.text:
The first question is what the user cannot do, or what has become slow. Missing or inconsistent data needs a check of the monitoring path before it can support a decision. Recent changes, errors, and scan findings can suggest a cause, but need confirmation from other evidence.

Before a change, the operator confirms its target and preconditions. After the change, the user-facing operation must work again. A successful command or a healthy Pod is only part of that check.

docs.title: Observe: Inspect
docs.text:
Automated checks perform most of Inspect. They detect failed or slow requests and collect the measurements that an operator needs to start an investigation.

For an HTTP service, Inspect may combine:

  • a synthetic request that fails or becomes slow
  • an SLO or error-budget burn-rate alert
  • request latency and error metrics
  • gateway and upstream timings
  • pod health and saturation
  • dependency signals
  • logs and recent deployment changes

Together, the results should show which operation is affected, when the problem started, and how many users or services it affects. A deployment shortly before the first error is worth checking, but timing alone does not establish the cause.

docs.title: Decide: Investigate
docs.text:
During Investigate, the operator compares measurements and logs to test possible causes. The tools supply evidence, but the operator decides whether it is enough to choose a response.

For a slow STAC request path, the operator may ask:

  • is APISIX adding latency, or reporting a slow upstream?
  • is the STAC application saturated or restarting?
  • is PostgreSQL slow or connection-limited?
  • did a recent change plausibly affect the service?
  • which action is safe enough to reduce the current user impact?

The investigation can continue after service has been restored. Once there is enough evidence for a safe action, the operator can proceed and leave deeper questions for the later review.

Saved dashboards, log queries, dependency checks, and procedures reduce the work needed during an incident. Queries need time and resource limits so that the investigation does not add unnecessary load.

docs.title: Change: Act and Verify
docs.text:
During Act, the approved procedure runs on the selected targets and within its limits. The planned remediation-action library will hold these procedures.

Verify is part of Act. After a workload restart, for example, the operator checks that the workload is healthy and repeats the external request. The relevant SLO signals must also recover and remain stable for a suitable period before the action is complete.

If verification fails, the system returns to investigation. It may stop, roll back, retry within a defined limit, or escalate, depending on the action.

docs.title: Improve: Learn
docs.text:
After recovery, Learn gives the team time to review the cause, timeline, action, and recovery checks. Missing or misleading measurements also belong in this review. The findings can lead to:

  • better metrics, SLOs, or synthetic checks
  • clearer investigation guidance
  • safer or more useful remediation actions
  • stronger preconditions and verification
  • follow-up changes that prevent recurrence

docs.title: Service Examples
docs.text: The STAC example starts with a slow HTTP request, and the workspace example starts with a slow session or failed data request. The control-plane example follows increased controller activity and its effect on the Kubernetes API. All three use the same investigation and recovery process.

docs.title: From Investigate to Act
docs.text: The remediation-action library is still in development. Each action will state when it can help, what it changes, who approves it, and how to check recovery.

docs.title: How the Current Stack Supports the Model
docs.text: Stage Current role Inspect Prometheus, SLO rules, synthetic checks, and health signals detect degradation. Alertmanager groups and routes the alerts. Investigate Keep presents alerts and context; Grafana, Loki, Kubernetes, and service-specific signals help the operator find the affected component. Act A small remediation-action library is in development. Existing scripts and procedures can run the actions. Verify Synthetics, workload health, and the same service signals used by Inspect confirm whether recovery occurred. Learn The incident record and observed outcomes improve monitoring, guidance, actions, and service design.

docs.title: Platform Lifecycle and Continuity Operations
docs.text: Platform changes need a record of what is deployed, who maintains it, and how to recover or retire it. Git and Argo CD provide configuration and deployment history. Service tests, support records, restore exercises, and retirement checks are also needed to show that a change is ready.

docs.title: Deployed Tools and Configuration
docs.text: Area Configuration and use Configuration source Platform and desired state Kubernetes runs the workloads. Argo CD applies the configuration from Git and reports drift, so changes can be reviewed and repeated. Argo CD desired state. Artifact evidence Argo CD records deployment sources, while Trivy supplies software inventory and vulnerability reports. These help with release and support decisions, but do not establish how an image was built. Deployment tree and Trivy Operator. Certificate lifecycle cert-manager issues and renews certificates. A ready certificate still needs a check through the public TLS route. Certificate configuration. Backup and restore RKE2 creates local platform snapshots, and some services have backup settings. There is no common backup inventory or restore procedure, so recovery still needs to be demonstrated. Platform configuration and service definitions in the deployment tree. Compatibility checks Repository workflows provide smoke and acceptance tests. Release checks need to exercise representative platform and service paths. CI workflows.

docs.title: Sign-off Evidence
docs.text:
The table records findings from the previous live review. Re-run the commands before sign-off, and save the results of restore, failure-domain, and retirement exercises. Configuration inspection alone cannot complete those checks.

✓ marks a deployed automated part of a check, rather than a passed check. An empty cell means the check needs manual work or has no automation.

Sign-off check Automated part Current state Next step Declarative inventory and drift ✓ Git and Argo CD provide a declared inventory and drift status. Ownership, support, and data-class information are incomplete. Add these fields to a small owned platform inventory and clear drift before release.kubectl get applications.argoproj.io -n argocd -o 'custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,SYNC:.status.sync.status,HEALTH:.status.health.status' Artifact and support trace ✓ Deployment sources and Trivy reports exist, but the record does not yet link source, build, and deployed image. Start with the operations namespace. Record the owner, support status, source, provenance, signature, and deployed image identity.kubectl get sbomreports.aquasecurity.github.io -n operations -o 'custom-columns=WORKLOAD:.metadata.labels.trivy-operator\.resource\.name,IMAGE:.report.artifact.repository,DIGEST:.report.artifact.digest,UPDATED:.report.updateTimestamp' Planned change ✓ GitOps and test workflows are in place, but no complete upgrade and rollback exercise has been saved. Run a representative upgrade and save health, compatibility, and rollback results. Isolated restore ✓ Local platform snapshots exist, but there is no common backup inventory or saved isolated restore test. Define the permitted data loss (RPO), recovery time (RTO), backup location, and owner for each data class, then test a restore.kubectl get etcdsnapshotfiles.k3s.cattle.io,volumesnapshots.snapshot.storage.k8s.io -A Disaster recovery No complete failure-domain exercise has been saved. Restore a minimum service in an isolated environment and measure recovery. Decommissioning No complete service-retirement exercise has been saved. Retire a disposable service and verify removal of access, routes, data, monitoring, and cost.

docs.title: Operator Detail
docs.text: The Operating Model explains approval and recovery checks for a change. Alerting and SLOs describes the service measurements that help judge whether a rollout has affected users.

docs.title: Reliability and Remediation Operations
docs.text: When a user cannot complete a request, reliability work starts with that failure. Measurements, logs, Kubernetes state, and recent GitOps changes help explain it. The operator then needs a procedure with clear limits and a way to check that the user can complete the request again.

docs.title: Deployed Tools and Configuration
docs.text: Area Configuration and use Configuration source Metrics and dashboards Prometheus collects platform and service measurements for Git-managed Grafana dashboards. Changes in health and load help locate the problem, but need other evidence to establish its cause. Monitoring and dashboards. Logs Alloy sends workload and selected node logs to Loki. These events can explain symptoms first seen in metrics or alerts. Loki and Alloy. Alerts and coordination Prometheus rules detect conditions that need attention. Alertmanager sends notifications to Keep, where operators can review related alerts and record the response. Rules and alerting. User-service checks The STAC synthetic checker sends regular requests and logs their status and timing. It tests the request path that internal Pod health cannot confirm. Deployment and check script. GitOps Argo CD applies the declared configuration and reports drift and reconciliation health. A successful sync still needs a separate service check. Argo CD tree.

docs.title: Sign-off Evidence
docs.text:
Previous tests checked that Keep retained alerts across a backend Pod replacement. Separate API/etcd and STAC test alerts then checked repeated delivery, acknowledgement, and resolution, with saved snapshots and Loki markers. Those alerts went directly to Keep: the tests did not cover the complete Alertmanager route or a remediation procedure.

The table records review results and the work still needed. Re-run the commands and review fresh results before sign-off. ✓ marks a deployed automated part of a check, rather than a passed check. An empty cell means the check needs manual work or has no automation.

Sign-off check Automated part Current state Next step User-facing health ✓ The STAC checker logs HTTP status, latency, and response checks. It does not publish a service-health metric. Review the latest request results, then publish a service-health metric.kubectl logs -n data-access deployment/synthetic-api-check --tail=20 Alert delivery ✓ Alertmanager routes alerts to Keep. Marked API/etcd and STAC alerts sent directly to Keep passed their workflow lifecycle checks. Retain a separate test through the complete Alertmanager delivery route.kubectl get alertmanagerconfig.monitoring.coreos.com keep -n operations -o 'custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,RECEIVER:.spec.route.receiver' Missing telemetry ✓ Prometheus can detect missing metric targets. Log-source freshness is not covered in the same way. Add missing-log detection and test the stale-source view. Investigation path The tools provide measurements, logs, and change history, but no timed service exercise has been saved. Run an exercise and record how the evidence was found and how long it took. Runbook execution General remediation guidance exists, but tested service runbooks are not yet available. Add a small set of service runbooks with stop and escalation conditions. Workflow control Git defines Keep workflows for enrichment and event logs. Production remediation workflows are not yet defined. Add a remediation workflow with approval, explicit targets, retry limits, and rollback rules. Keep remediation Keep records the response, but no remediation run has been saved. Test that workflow against a safe fault and save the result. Recovery ✓ Metrics and synthetic checks can show recovery, but no complete recovery record has been saved. Define how long recovery must remain stable and use these checks after the workflow test. GitOps reconciliation ✓ Argo CD reports desired-state health, but no change and drift exercise has been saved. Test a reviewed change and safe drift, then save the reconciliation result.kubectl get applications.argoproj.io -n argocd -o 'custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,SYNC:.status.sync.status,HEALTH:.status.health.status' Incident record and learning The tools can supply a timeline; no complete exercise record brings it together yet. Link the alert, decision, action, recovery checks, and follow-up work in one record.

docs.title: Operator Detail
docs.text:
Observability Basics explains what metrics, logs, and alerts can tell you. The dashboard guide covers the available views, and Remediation Actions describes the planned action library.

The STAC, workspace, and control-plane scenarios follow specific problems from the first report through investigation and recovery checks.

docs.title: Remediation Actions
docs.text:
A RemediationAction will describe a prepared procedure: when it may help, what it can change, and how to check the result. An operator will select and approve it after investigating the problem.

In development

The library is not deployed. This page describes its intended use; the API, resource model, and execution design are still open.

docs.title: Why Use an Action Library?
docs.text:
Preparing a procedure before an incident gives the operator time to review its targets, risks, and recovery checks. It could run through a script, Kubernetes operation, workflow, or API call. The library will describe the required result and the limits that apply, regardless of how the procedure runs.

Read-only checks may run automatically. A production change will require human approval, explicit targets, execution and retry limits, and a service-level recovery check. Destructive changes, changes to data, and identity or access operations remain outside the ordinary library.

docs.title: What an Action Needs to Explain
docs.text:
Before an action can be used, its procedure must explain:

  • its intended outcome and when it may help
  • the permitted services and targets
  • its preconditions and execution limits
  • the required approval and execution method
  • how recovery is verified
  • when to stop, roll back, or return to Investigate

docs.title: The Action Flow
docs.text:
1. Select: The operator chooses an action based on the investigation.
  2. Check and approve: The operator confirms the target and preconditions, then approves the change.
  3. Execute: The procedure runs within its defined limits.
  4. Verify: Health checks and a user-facing request confirm whether the service has recovered.
  5. Record: The incident record keeps the evidence, approval, execution details, and result for later review.

If the recovery check fails, the response returns to Investigate or follows the procedure’s stop, rollback, retry, or escalation instructions.

docs.title: Example: Restart a Stateless Workload
docs.text: Question Example answer What does it do? Replace the running replicas of a selected stateless workload. When may it help? Replicas are unhealthy or stuck and replacement is a reasonable mitigation. What is checked first? The target is stateless, no rollout is active, and enough capacity remains. Who approves it? A human operator. How is it verified? Replicas become healthy, the external service request succeeds, and relevant SLO signals recover. What if it fails? Stop repeated attempts and return to Investigate or escalate.

docs.title: Security Operations
docs.text: Security work includes checking workload settings, reviewing scan findings, controlling access, and responding to suspicious activity. The controls below cover different parts of this work. Their presence alone does not establish that the platform has passed a security review.

docs.title: Deployed Tools and Configuration
docs.text: Control Configuration and use Configuration source Workload admission Pod Security Admission audits and warns about Restricted settings. Kyverno adds policy reports, exceptions, and application policies. These checks evaluate Kubernetes resources during admission. Namespace configuration and Kyverno policies. Security scanning Trivy Operator scans for vulnerabilities, configuration, RBAC, and compliance findings. It stores Kubernetes reports for review; it does not block activity in running workloads. Trivy Operator. Runtime detection Falco, which detects suspicious activity in running workloads, is not deployed. Identity and gateway Keycloak authenticates users, OPA and OPAL supply authorization policy, and APISIX enforces access on protected HTTP routes. These controls cover service requests; Kubernetes API access has separate controls. IAM and APISIX. Cluster access RBAC limits actions through the Kubernetes API. NetworkPolicy limits network paths between Pods and services. Service definitions in the Argo CD tree. Secrets and certificates Sealed Secrets and External Secrets deliver workload secrets. cert-manager issues and renews TLS certificates. Sealed Secrets, External Secrets, and certificates. Evidence and response Alloy and Loki provide logs for investigation, alongside Prometheus metrics in Grafana. Alertmanager sends notifications to Keep, where operators record the response. Monitoring, rules, and alerting.

docs.title: Sign-off Evidence
docs.text:
The table records findings from the previous live review and the work still needed. Re-run the commands and review fresh results before sign-off.

✓ marks a deployed automated part of a check, rather than a passed check. An empty cell means the check needs manual work or has no automation.

Sign-off check Automated part Current state Next step Platform and node identity ✓ Kubernetes reports node identity, role, and readiness. Save the inventory with the sign-off record.kubectl get nodes -o wide CIS coverage ✓ Trivy produces node compliance reports with findings that need review. Review each finding and record its resolution or approved exception.kubectl get clustercompliancereports.aquasecurity.github.io -o 'custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,UPDATED:.status.updateTimestamp,PASS:.status.summary.passCount,FAIL:.status.summary.failCount' Pod admission ✓ Pod Security Admission and Kyverno evaluate Restricted controls in audit mode. Resolve reported findings, then test a controlled move to enforcement.kubectl get policyreports.wgpolicyk8s.io -A -o 'custom-columns=NAMESPACE:.metadata.namespace,KIND:.scope.kind,RESOURCE:.scope.name,POLICY:.results[0].policy,PASS:.summary.pass,FAIL:.summary.fail' Fail-closed admission ✓ The main Restricted policy permits admission when its webhook is unavailable. Agree on the failure policy and test it before enforcement.kubectl get clusterpolicy.kyverno.io pod-security-restricted-audit -o 'custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,READY:.status.conditions[?(@.type=="Ready")].status,FAILURE-POLICY:.spec.failurePolicy,ACTION:.spec.rules[0].validate.failureAction' Trivy coverage and freshness ✓ Workload and compliance reports are produced, with alerts for findings that need attention. Match deployed workloads to fresh reports and review high-priority findings.kubectl get vulnerabilityreports.aquasecurity.github.io -A -o 'custom-columns=NAMESPACE:.metadata.namespace,WORKLOAD:.metadata.labels.trivy-operator\.resource\.name,UPDATED:.report.updateTimestamp,CRITICAL:.report.summary.criticalCount,HIGH:.report.summary.highCount' Exceptions Kyverno exceptions include scope, owner, reason, and review information. Other security exceptions are less consistent. Use the same exception record for policy, scan, and compliance findings.kubectl get policyexceptions.kyverno.io -A -o 'custom-columns=NAMESPACE:.metadata.namespace,NAME:.metadata.name,OWNER:.metadata.annotations.security\.eoepca\.org/owner,REASON:.metadata.annotations.security\.eoepca\.org/reason,REVIEW-AFTER:.metadata.annotations.security\.eoepca\.org/review-after' Falco coverage and delivery Falco is not deployed. Deploy runtime detection and test delivery, or record an approved alternative.kubectl get daemonsets -A -l app.kubernetes.io/name=falco Kubernetes API audit ✓ Audit collection and alert rules are configured, but current audit records are not available in Loki yet. Restore audit delivery and test one allowed and one denied action. Identity and gateway enforcement ✓ Keycloak, OPA, OPAL, and APISIX are deployed, but no saved access test confirms enforcement. Record allowed, denied, and direct-backend request tests. RBAC and network boundaries ✓ RBAC and NetworkPolicy are configured. Approved access paths and probe results have not been collected in one record. Record the approved paths and test one allowed and one denied path. Secret handling ✓ Secret controllers are deployed, but no delivery and leakage test has been saved. Test a safe marker from source to workload and confirm that it does not appear in Git or logs. Certificate issue and use ✓ Certificate resources report ready, and the public TLS path was valid during inspection. Keep a renewal alert and repeat the external TLS check before sign-off.kubectl get certificates.cert-manager.io -A Dashboard freshness and detail ✓ Security dashboards and report-freshness alerts exist. Log-source freshness is incomplete. Add log-source freshness detection and test dashboard drill-down.

docs.title: Operator Detail
docs.text: The dashboard guide explains how to review security findings and report age. The alerting reference covers their delivery to Keep.

docs.title: ServiceMonitors and PodMonitors
docs.text: A metrics endpoint does not become part of monitoring just because a Pod exposes it. Prometheus must discover and scrape it. A ServiceMonitor selects a Kubernetes Service and its metrics port; a PodMonitor selects Pods directly.

docs.title: Why ServiceMonitors Matter
docs.text: A ServiceMonitor gives Prometheus Operator a managed target definition, including the endpoint and scrape settings. Once selected by Prometheus, that target supplies the metrics used by dashboards, alerts, and SLO calculations.

docs.title: Why the Operations BB Uses Them
docs.text: The Operations BB keeps target definitions with service configuration rather than maintaining a separate list of scrape endpoints. Teams can add a service’s metrics endpoint and monitor resource together, under the same review.

docs.title: What is Scraped Today
docs.text:
In eoepca-demo, ServiceMonitors are defined in:

  • operations for the monitoring and alerting stack
  • ingress-apisix for APISIX metrics
  • infra for PostgreSQL exporter metrics
  • data-access for operation-specific stac-auth-proxy metrics

Examples from the current deployment:

  • eoepca/data-access/parts/servicemonitor-stac-auth-proxy.yaml scrapes STAC request and latency metrics
  • infra/pgo/parts/servicemonitor-postgres-exporter.yaml scrapes PostgreSQL exporter metrics
  • infra/apisix/parts/servicemonitor-apisix.yaml scrapes APISIX metrics from /apisix/prometheus/metrics
  • app-keep-oauth2-proxy.yaml enables a chart-managed ServiceMonitor for the Keep proxy
  • app-loki-stack.yaml enables Loki monitoring integration

The live operations namespace currently has ServiceMonitors for:

  • Alloy log collection
  • Crossplane core controller metrics
  • Keep OAuth2 proxy metrics
  • kube-prometheus-stack components, including Alertmanager, Grafana, Prometheus, kube-state-metrics, kubelet, and node exporter
  • Loki-related chart-managed metrics

docs.title: Crossplane Metrics
docs.text:
The crossplane-core ServiceMonitor and crossplane-providers PodMonitor in operations select controllers in infra. They collect client request counters for the Kubernetes API and etcd dashboard and alert snapshots.

These client counters help identify controller traffic. The API’s resource breakdown shows which objects were accessed, but cannot identify the caller by itself. The monitor definitions are in crossplane-metrics.yaml.

docs.title: Workspace PodMonitor
docs.text:
The workspace-managed-data PodMonitor in operations selects package-r pods across workspace namespaces and scrapes /metrics. This keeps managed data collection in step with workspace Pod creation and removal. The workspace provider also creates the network policy that allows Prometheus to reach the metrics port.

The workspace scenario explains how these metrics and the workspace recording rules supply the dashboard. The PodMonitor definition is in workspace-managed-data.yaml.

The demo also has the infra/pods-by-annotation PodMonitor.

docs.title: Concrete Example: Database Pod
docs.text:
The PostgreSQL database Pod in infra shows how the pieces connect:

  • the Crunchy PostgresCluster enables the pgmonitor exporter
  • the running database pod includes an exporter container with a named exporter port on 9187
  • the default-pods headless Service selects pods with postgres-operator.crunchydata.com/cluster: default
  • the postgres-exporter ServiceMonitor selects that Service and scrapes the exporter target port every 30s

Relevant files:

  • postgrescluster.yaml enables the PostgreSQL monitoring exporter
  • servicemonitor-postgres-exporter.yaml defines the scrape target

This supplies PostgreSQL exporter and pg_stat_statements measurements for comparison with STAC request latency.

docs.title: Metric Labels
docs.text:
Metric labels need a controlled set of values. A label containing every full request URL would create too many separate time series. APISIX instead uses labels such as route and HTTP method, configured in infra/apisix/parts/values/apisix-values.yaml.

The STAC auth proxy uses operation, method, and status labels to distinguish searches and other STAC operations without full request URLs. The STAC end-to-end example shows how these metrics complement gateway, workload, database, log, and synthetic signals.

docs.title: When a STAC Request Slows Down
docs.text:
A user reports slow or failed STAC searches. The request passes through APISIX, the authorisation proxy, the STAC API, and PostgreSQL/pgSTAC. Comparing these layers helps locate the delay or failure.

The demo’s public endpoint is https://eoapi.develop-v2.eoepca.org/stac. The target is 99% of GET and POST requests within 500 ms. A burn-rate alert fires when the share of slow requests is too high.

For this example, we increased the synthetic STAC checker from two to 40 replicas. More requests reached the public endpoint, latency rose, and the GET and POST critical alerts fired. Alertmanager sent them to Keep through the normal alert route. The alert rules stayed unchanged.

docs.title: Review the Alert in Keep
docs.text:
In the Keep alert feed, look for a STAC GET or POST latency alert around the time of the user’s report. Its operation helps narrow the investigation to the affected requests. When you take an alert, assign it to yourself and acknowledge it so other operators can see that someone is handling it.

Keep enriches a new firing alert with a snapshot from the gateway, proxy, API, and database. The alert’s Grafana link opens charts for that period, while the saved values remain in Keep after acknowledgement and resolution.

Open the alert, select View Alert, then enable Enriched Fields Only to see the saved links and measurements.

The screenshot shows the GET alert with its saved measurements. Keep also received the POST alert from the same load test.

docs.title: Compare Events with the Charts
docs.text:
Follow the alert’s Grafana link to compare the saved values with the charts before and after the notification. If you open the STAC dashboard directly, set its time range to the incident period.

Keep events is on by default. It adds blue markers when Keep handles a firing or resolved notification. Hover over a marker to see its time, status, and link back to the alert. These markers come from Keep’s event log, which Alloy sends to Loki for Grafana to read. The saved measurements stay in Keep.

Turning Keep events off gives the same charts without the markers, as shown below. This only changes the display; metrics and alert delivery continue.

Signal What to check APISIX ingress Are public requests slow or failing? Compare request, upstream, and gateway latency with GET/POST budget burn. Auth proxy Did errors or latency rise for the affected STAC operation? STAC API Does the backend show the same delay, errors, or workload pressure? Database Did mean query latency rise in the shared eoapi database?

The ingress panels are the starting point because the alert rules measure this public route. Comparing them with the proxy and API panels shows whether the delay is also visible further along the request path. Logs from that period can give request details. If both services slow down, the database or another shared dependency may need investigation.

The same request can appear at several layers, so adding their counts would count it more than once. Their p99 values may describe different requests; subtracting them does not give the delay between layers. The database mean also covers the shared database, rather than STAC alone. An empty panel needs a collection check before it can support a conclusion. Marker times include notification delay.

docs.title: Check Recovery
docs.text:
We returned the checker to two replicas after the alerts fired. Traffic and latency fell, but the alerts stayed firing because their one-hour window still included the slow requests.

After an approved change, repeat the user’s search through the public endpoint. Successful requests, including the synthetic checks, and lower errors and latency show whether the change helped. These need to remain stable before the incident is closed. The burn rate can take longer to fall because its window still includes older slow requests; a ready Pod or resolved alert alone does not confirm recovery.

The Keep record should explain what changed, whether it helped, and which measurements were missing. If several services are affected together, the control-plane scenario helps investigate the Kubernetes API as a shared dependency.

The dashboard guide and alerting reference describe the measurements and shared workflows. The STAC rules and synthetic checker define the service checks. The remediation-action library is still in development.

docs.title: Workspace Monitoring
docs.text: When a session is slow or a data request fails, the Workspaces dashboard brings together the sessions, namespaces, and managed data activity for that workspace.

docs.title: What the Dashboard Shows
docs.text:
Selecting a workspace and the reported time shows its running sessions, CPU and memory use, requested PVC storage, and owned buckets. Shared services count once in workspace totals. The managed data panels show whether requests or presigned URLs failed, how much data was transferred, and whether metrics are being collected.

PVC requests show allocated capacity, and transfer bytes measure data movement. Neither shows how much data is stored. Used storage and exact outgoing S3 request counts are not measured per workspace.

docs.title: How Metrics Reach the Dashboard
docs.text:
The recording rules in workspace-metrics.yaml link workspace inventory, namespaces, sessions, and pods. The dashboard reuses this mapping so that each panel includes the same workspace resources.

The workspace-managed-data PodMonitor collects managed data activity from package-r pods across workspace namespaces. The workspace provider creates a network policy that permits Prometheus to reach the metrics port.

docs.title: Example: A Slow Session or Failed Data Request
docs.text:
Start with the workspace and the time reported by the user. Session CPU and memory use may show resource pressure, while the managed data panels may show failed requests. If a panel is empty, collection health needs checking before the absence of data can be interpreted.

The session table identifies the pods whose logs can help explain a slow session. For a failed data request, package-r logs and bucket access checks can help locate the failure.

After an approved change, repeating the user’s request tests whether it helped. Errors and resource use should also recover; Pod readiness alone does not show that the session or data access works. The incident record should include the cause, change, result, and any missing measurements for the later review.
